text: It's easy to think of cybersecurity as purely digital — firewalls, encryption, malware. But the CIA triad doesn't care whether a threat is physical or digital. If someone walks into a server room and removes a drive, that's a confidentiality failure, because the data on it is now exposed, and an availability failure at the same time, because whatever depended on that drive is now down. No firewall rule matters if an attacker can just walk up to the hardware.

Physical access controls layer the same way the technical ones did. Badge access restricts entry and logs who went in, where, and when. Mantraps are interlocking doors that verify one person at a time, so an unauthorized person can't tailgate in behind someone authorized. Security cameras cover entrances and server rooms as both a deterrent and evidence afterward. And visitor logs record every non-employee who enters, with a time in, time out, and who they were visiting.

Getting into the room isn't the only risk — the environment inside it threatens hardware too. HVAC and cooling keep server rooms within a safe temperature and humidity range, because servers generate enormous heat and will fail without it. Fire suppression systems use specialized agents instead of water, so a fire gets put out without destroying the electronics. And UPS battery backup bridges a power outage for long enough that systems shut down gracefully or a generator takes over.

That drive-theft example is really the whole lesson in miniature: one physical failure, two triad violations at once, and no amount of network-side security prevents either one. Even cloud-first companies still depend on this layer — it's just the provider managing the badges, cameras, and generators instead of the company itself.

That closes out the policy and defense-in-depth chapter. Next up, Chapter 8 moves from theory to hands-on practice, starting with building a home lab where you can actually apply everything from this course.
